Key takeaways


AI agents are autonomous software systems that can perform tasks such as donor outreach, volunteer coordination, and grant research on behalf of nonprofit staff, and they require identity-based security to protect sensitive stakeholder data.


Nonprofits can safely deploy AI agents by treating them as managed identities, enforcing least-privilege access, and requiring human approval for sensitive actions.


The biggest security risks for nonprofit AI agents include identity debt, prompt injection, and overprivileged access—all of which are preventable with proper identity governance.


According to the Center for Effective Philanthropy, 90% of nonprofits express interest in increasing their use of AI, with communications (84%) and internal productivity (63%) as top priorities.


This guide is for nonprofit technology leaders, IT administrators, and executive directors evaluating the adoption and security of AI agents.


## Nonprofit capacity gaps and the AI agent revolution


**The challenge:** Nonprofits operate under tremendous pressure while pursuing extensive mission-critical goals. With limited resources for technology and training, repetitive yet necessary tasks—such as email management, reporting, and volunteer coordination—can impede staff productivity.


**The opportunity:** AI agents—autonomous software systems that perform tasks such as donor outreach, volunteer coordination, and grant research on behalf of nonprofit staff—can be the impact multiplier mission-driven organizations need. They act as autonomous digital staff, handling high-touch workflows like personalized donor communications and grant proposals.


**The security imperative:** To trust these powerful new agents with sensitive stakeholder data, such as personally identifiable information (PII) or financial details of donors and beneficiaries, nonprofits must ground their AI strategy in a[strong security framework](https://www.okta.com/solutions/secure-ai/agentic-enterprise-blueprint/) . By securing the identities and actions of AI agents, nonprofits can unlock massive efficiency gains while avoiding preventable risks such as identity debt, prompt injection, and overprivileged access.


## Top AI agent security risks for nonprofits


### Identity debt


Identity debt occurs when AI agents rely on static, long-lived API keys that are rarely rotated, creating persistent "secret sprawl" that attackers can harvest. For example, if a fundraising agent uses a permanent API key to access your donor database and that key is stolen, attackers gain an invisible backdoor to sensitive financial records.


### Prompt injection


Prompt injection is a technique where bad actors hide malicious instructions in donor emails or grant text, allowing them to hijack an agent's logic and bypass security rules. A grant research agent could be tricked into revealing confidential information or performing unauthorized actions.


### Overprivileged access


Overprivileged access happens when agents are given super admin rights to be helpful, creating a massive blast radius if compromised. A grant research agent with read-all access could inadvertently pull and summarize sensitive board meeting minutes or employee salary data when tricked by a malicious prompt.


## Securing AI agents and staying in control


Understanding these risks is the first step toward securing your mission. Here are some considerations to be mindful of:


- **Secure connections:** AI agents should be securely connected to apps and data
- **Stakeholder control:** Your stakeholders should have control over the actions AI agents can perform and the data they can access
- **Human confirmation:** Humans should confirm critical agent actions
- **Unmanaged agent detection:** Identify unmanaged AI agents before they can lead to a breach
- **Identity-first approach:** Every AI agent, script, and service account should be treated as an identity


By treating[agents as non-human identities](https://www.okta.com/blog/ai/how-do-you-govern-an-ai-agent-identity-and-why-it-matters/) (digital entities that require authentication and authorization, similar to employees), you can enjoy the speed of AI without the "insider threat" risk.


## How can AI agents empower your team?


Building an AI agent or even an AI strategy can be a substantial undertaking, especially when your team is resource-constrained. But AI investments can pay significant dividends.


In 2025, the nonprofit Sage Future[tasked four AI models](https://techcrunch.com/2025/04/08/a-nonprofit-is-using-ai-agents-to-raise-money-for-charity/) with raising money for Helen Keller International. Sage Director Adam Binksmith says the experiment is a useful illustration of agents’ current capabilities and the rate at which they’re improving. Even as a work in progress, the benefits of AI strategies may be huge.


According to the Center for Effective Philanthropy’s[AI with Purpose 2025](https://cep.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/CEP_AI_Layout_FINAL.pdf) report, 90% of nonprofits express interest in increasing their organization’s use of AI. Their most common use cases include:


- Communications: 84%
- Internal productivity: 63%
- Development and fundraising: 61%


Earlier this year, our[Okta for Good](https://www.okta.com/company/okta-for-good/) team conducted a[focused assessment](https://www.okta.com/newsroom/articles/scaling-nonprofit-missions-safely-in-the-ai-era/) , interviewing more than 20 nonprofit leaders, tech funders, and AI experts across our ecosystem. The study found that AI’s core value lies in creating additional staff capacity. While AI maturity may vary, industry leaders widely acknowledge AI’s potential to add value.


## How can AI agents increase capacity for resource-constrained nonprofits?


AI agents can help your team automate manual or repetitive work and boost productivity across several key areas:


- **Automating mundane tasks:** Offload scheduling, data entry, and frequent internal inquiries so your team can dedicate more time to high-touch, impactful work.
- **Handling stakeholder requests:** Answer common questions and deliver service information promptly to help you reach those who need support most, wherever and whenever.
- **Offering strategic insights in real time:** Process large volumes of data quickly to provide predictive models that inform service delivery and maximize your impact.


Now, let’s dive into more examples.


## AI use cases


Area What type of agent could you build? How it empowers your team


**Fundraising and donor relations** **Personalized donor agent:** Drafts personalized thank-you notes, schedules follow-up calls based on giving history, and processes instant donor acknowledgments. This agent can strengthen donor loyalty and increase retention rates. Your donor relations team can use the saved time to add a personal touch to each communication.


**Operations** **Volunteer manager agent:** Automates volunteer onboarding, coordinates shift schedules, sends reminders, and manages sign-up forms. This agent can reduce administrative burden and improve the volunteer experience, building a strong community pipeline.


**Program and service delivery** **Grant research agent:** Searches for relevant grant opportunities based on mission criteria, tracks deadlines, and drafts proposal outlines. This agent can accelerate funding acquisition and expand your development team’s research capacity.


**Internal efficiency** **Reporting agent:** Gathers data from multiple systems (CRM, finance, service metrics) to automatically generate real-time performance dashboards for board members. This agent can save hours of manual reporting work and enable faster, data-driven decisions for your board and other stakeholders.

## Frequently asked questions


###


AI agents are autonomous software systems that perform tasks like donor outreach, volunteer coordination, grant research, and reporting on behalf of nonprofit staff. They act as digital team members that handle repetitive workflows while staff focus on high-impact work.


###


The main risks include identity debt (unmanaged API keys creating backdoors), prompt injection (malicious instructions hidden in text that hijack agent behavior), and overprivileged access (agents with excessive permissions that expand the blast radius of a breach).


###


Nonprofits can secure AI agents by treating them as managed non-human identities, enforcing least-privilege access, requiring human-in-the-loop approvals for sensitive actions, and continuously monitoring agent activity with unified identity governance.
